text_blocks.snippet: Lyme disease bloodwork typically involves a two-tiered testing approach to detect antibodies produced in response to the Borrelia burgdorferi bacteria, which is the cause of Lyme disease. The process usually starts with an ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) test, and if positive or indeterminate, a Western blot test is performed to confirm the results.
snippet_highlighted_words: typically involves a two-tiered testing approach to detect antibodies produced in response to the Borrelia burgdorferi bacteria

list.title: ELISA Test:
list.snippet: This is the initial screening test that looks for antibodies to Borrelia burgdorferi in the blood.

list.title: Western Blot Test:
list.snippet: If the ELISA test is positive or unclear, the Western blot test is performed to confirm the presence of Lyme disease antibodies. It identifies specific antibodies against different proteins of the bacteria.

list.title: Antibodies:
list.snippet: The Lyme disease bacteria trigger the immune system to produce antibodies, which are proteins that fight off the infection. The ELISA and Western blot tests detect these antibodies in the blood.

list.title: When to Test:
list.snippet: Antibody tests are most reliable after Lyme disease has been present for a few weeks, as it takes time for the body to produce detectable antibodies.

list.title: Spinal Tap:
list.snippet: In some cases, a spinal tap (lumbar puncture) may be necessary to obtain cerebrospinal fluid for testing, particularly if Lyme disease is suspected to have affected the nervous system.

list.title: Other Tests:
list.snippet: In certain situations, additional tests like PCR (polymerase chain reaction) for detecting bacterial DNA or other specialized tests may be used, especially if the standard tests are inconclusive or if the infection is suspected to be in a very early or late stage, according to Long Island Lyme Disease.
